newsitem.title: USA: Mission control dismisses glitch on U.S. shuttle.
newsitem.headline: Mission control dismisses glitch on U.S. shuttle.

text.p: The U.S. space shuttle Columbia has developed strange readings from one of its three electricity-generating fuel cells, but mission control said on Friday they were probably caused by a bad transistor in the monitoring system.

NASA's first attempt to fly the current science mission was cut short in April after only five days because of a faulty fuel cell. Mission control assured the crew that there would not be a repeat of that incident.
"We're 100 percent positive that it's just a (monitoring) problem," spacecraft communicator Bill McArthur told shuttle skipper Jim Halsell.
Flight controllers told the crew they might get a chance to chat with fellow NASA astronaut Mike Foale aboard the troubled Mir space station.

A linkup by amateur radio -- both Columbia and Mir are carrying "radio ham"-style devices -- should be possible when the two craft pass within 70 miles (110 km) of each other shortly before 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT) on Saturday.
Columbia blasted off from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre on Tuesday. The crew of seven is working on a $86 million research programme in a laboratory mounted in the shuttle's cargo bay.

The shuttle crew earlier on Friday applauded news that the Mars Pathfinder probe had landed. Mission control radioed the news to the crew shortly after the probe landed on the surface of the Red Planet.
Flight controllers in Houston planned to beam the first images from the Mars probe to the shuttle later on Friday, NASA spokesman Kyle Herring said.
In an interview for CNN International, Halsell and his crew said they were ready to sign up for the first manned mission to Mars.
"You bet," astronaut Janice Voss called down.
Co-pilot Susan Still was not so sure. "Maybe," she said.
